h1: Ageing beer bottles upright or on their side
title: Age Beer Bottles Upright or Sideways? | Craft Beer School
desc: Should you age beer upright or on its side? What crown caps, corks, yeast sediment and oxygen mean for how bottles are stored.
teaser: Wine lies down. Beer, with a few exceptions, stands up. Here is why.
standfirst: Wine collectors store bottles on their side, so many beer drinkers assume they should too. For most beer the opposite is true. Here is the reasoning, plus the case for the few corked beers that are different.
sections:
For almost all beer, store bottles upright. That covers crown-capped bottles, which is most beer in India and around the world. It applies whether you are keeping beer for a month or for several years.

The reasons are practical. Yeast sediment settles neatly at the bottom. Less beer touches the cap. The surface where beer meets the air in the neck is smaller. Each of these helps the beer age more cleanly and pour more clearly.
Sediment settles where you want it

Bottle-conditioned beers, such as many Belgian ales, contain live yeast that settles as a layer at the bottom of the bottle. Stored upright, the yeast forms a compact cake that stays put when you pour carefully. Stored on its side, it spreads along the length of the bottle and stirs into the beer as soon as you lift it.

Even filtered beers can throw a little sediment over long ageing, as proteins and polyphenols slowly drop out. Upright storage keeps that out of the glass too.

A crown cap has a thin plastic liner that seals against the glass. There is no benefit in soaking that liner in beer for months. If a cap starts to rust or the seal is slightly weak, a bottle lying down puts beer right against the weak point. A bottle standing up keeps a cushion of gas between the two.

Lying a bottle down spreads the headspace into a long bubble along its side. That increases the area where beer meets whatever oxygen is in the bottle. It is a small effect, but over months and years oxygen is what turns malt flavours to cardboard and sherry.

Upright, the headspace is a small disc in the neck. The beer exposed to it is minimal.

Some Belgian ales, lambics and gueuzes come in corked bottles, often with a cage, like Champagne. Wine logic says lay them down to keep the cork moist so it does not shrink and let air in.

For beer, opinion is divided. Many brewers and experienced cellar keepers still store corked beer upright for months or even a year or two. If the cellar humidity is reasonable, around 50 to 70%, the cork stays moist enough from the air and the beer vapour in the headspace. Lying down for many years can make sense for bottles meant for very long ageing, but it brings the sediment problem back. If you do, stand the bottle up for a day or two before opening so the yeast settles.

Cork brings a small risk of cork taint, a musty note from a compound called TCA. Our piece on cork taint in beer explains how it happens.

Cans should also be stored upright, mostly for convenience, but the logic about headspace and liner contact applies too. Cans protect beer from light completely, which is a real advantage for hoppy beers. Large bottles such as 750 ml Belgian bottles are stored the same way as smaller ones.

Whatever the format, temperature matters far more than orientation. A bottle stored perfectly upright at 32 °C will age worse than one lying down at 12 °C.

All that care is wasted if the pour stirs up the sediment. Take the bottle out of the cooler gently and keep it upright. If it has been on its side, stand it up for a day or two first.

Let strong beers warm for 10 to 20 minutes, to around 10 to 13 °C, so the aroma opens up. Pour slowly in one continuous motion into a tilted glass, watching the neck. Stop when the cloudy layer of yeast reaches the shoulder of the bottle. Leave the last centimetre or so behind.

Some people like to drink the yeast separately or stir it in for a hefeweizen. For an aged Belgian ale or barley wine it usually adds a muddy, bitter edge, so most drinkers leave it. A snifter or tulip glass of 250 to 350 ml suits most aged beers: big enough to swirl, small enough to keep the pour modest.

The best way to settle the question for your own cellar is to taste. Buy two bottles of a strong, bottle-conditioned Belgian ale. Store one upright and one on its side, both at the same steady temperature, for six months.

Pour them side by side into clear glasses. Compare clarity, aroma and flavour. You will almost certainly see the difference in sediment. You may taste it too. Your first step is buying those two bottles and labelling one 'upright' and one 'side' with today's date.
faqs: Should beer bottles be stored upright?
Yes, for most beer. Upright storage keeps sediment at the bottom, limits contact with the cap and reduces the surface exposed to headspace oxygen.
Many cellar keepers still store corked beer upright for a year or two if humidity is reasonable. For very long ageing some lay it down, then stand it up before opening.
Does storing beer on its side ruin it?
Not usually, but sediment spreads through the bottle and the beer has more contact with the cap and headspace.
Does orientation matter more than temperature?
No. Temperature matters far more. A steady 10 to 13 °C is the main goal for ageing beer.
